body_markdown:
Working globally has taught me that one of the biggest challenges in communication isn’t language; it’s assumptions.


As someone who was raised in Germany and has spent much of my career in the United States, I’ve experienced how culture influences everything from communication styles to decision-making. Over the years, I’ve learned that understanding those differences can strengthen collaboration, but only if we approach them with the right mindset.


That’s why I found the Culture Map Assessment valuable.


What I appreciated most wasn’t that it tried to define me. Instead, it helped explain why certain communication habits felt natural while also highlighting how I had adapted over time. I realized I still communicate quite directly, a common characteristic of my German heritage, but I had also intentionally adopted communication styles that better support collaboration in the United States.


Today, I often use the Culture Map while mentoring leaders who work across different countries and cultures. It creates meaningful conversations about how people may approach communication differently and how we can adapt without losing authenticity.


The important part is remembering that culture explains tendencies, not individuals.


No assessment can fully describe a person. Every individual is shaped by experiences, personality, values and countless other influences. Cultural frameworks are most useful when they encourage curiosity rather than reinforce stereotypes.


Much of what I’ve learned didn’t come from assessments at all. It came from experience.


Sometimes people misunderstood what I meant. Other times I noticed my communication wasn’t having the intended effect. Those moments became opportunities to adjust and become more effective. Over time, I discovered that successful cross-cultural communication requires both self-awareness and humility.


I’ve also learned that feedback is one of the greatest gifts we can receive. When someone feels comfortable asking clarifying questions or offering constructive feedback, we have the chance to improve. That kind of honesty only exists when trust has been built.


Trust grows through consistency and genuine curiosity about other people. It grows when we invite honest conversations and demonstrate that feedback won’t be met with defensiveness.


[Global organizations](https://novanta.com/about/our-locations/) succeed because they bring together different perspectives. The more we seek to understand before being understood, the stronger our[collaboration](https://novanta.com/careers-culture/life-at-novanta/) becomes.
